Instructions for submitting Observer reports 
Introduction 
This document provides the reporting template and instructions for Observers to report 
during the 2023 - 2025 Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council. 

The deadline for submission is 1 December 2024. 
 

Role of Observers 
The role and responsibilities of Observers as well as the criteria for admission to the Arctic 
Council can be found in the “Arctic Council Rules of Procedure” (Annex 2) and the “Observer 
Manual for Subsidiary Bodies.” 

The primary role of Observers is to observe the work of the Arctic Council. Observers 
contribute to the Arctic Council primarily through engagement at the level of Working 
Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Observers are invited to the meetings and other 
activities of the Arctic Council unless the Senior Arctic Officials decide otherwise. Observers 
may also propose projects through an Arctic State or a Permanent Participant. 

Report submission 
Observer reports should include the relevant information described below and in the 
template. 

(a) A description of the Observer’s contributions to the work of the Arctic Council since 
the time of the Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years, with 
special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies through project participation 
and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent Participants; 

(b) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s future plans to contribute to the work of 
the Arctic Council, with special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies through 
project participation and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent 
Participants; and, 

(c) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s contributions to other aspects of the 
Arctic Council and its goals not covered in the previous sections since the time of the 
Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years. 

 

Observer reports should be submitted electronically to the Arctic Council Secretariat via 
email: acs@arctic-council.org not later than 1 December 2024. Please bear in mind while 
preparing your report that all Observer reports will be published online in the Observer 
section of the Arctic Council online Library (OAR) following the Chairship transition. 

If an Observer fails to submit a report, the Arctic Council will consider this to mean that the 
Observer is no longer interested in maintaining its status as an accredited Observer to 
the Arctic Council.

Observer Report 
This report is submitted in line with the EU's application for observer status from 2012, which is 
maintained, and the Arctic Council's decision to extend a standing invitation for the EU to attend 
its sessions at all levels. 
EU ARCTIC POLICY 
On 13 October 2021, the EU updated its Arctic policy under the Joint Communication on “A 
stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic” (JOIN(2021) 27 
final). The EU Arctic policy focuses on climate change and its impacts, safeguarding the Arctic 
environment and promoting sustainable development in the Arctic to the benefit of local 
inhabitants including indigenous peoples, and supporting international cooperation on Arctic 
matters. The EU Arctic policy highlights the defining role which climate change and its impacts 
play in all Arctic affairs. 
Since its 2023 report to the Arctic Council, the EU has kept implementing its 2021 Arctic policy. 
Major developments include the inauguration of the European Commission Office in Greenland 
(2024), the organisation of the EU Arctic Forum and Indigenous Peoples’ Dialogue in Nuuk, 
Greenland (2023) and Brussels, Belgium (2024), or the launch of the Copernicus Arctic Hub 
(2024). 
As part of its engagement with people living in the Arctic, in 2024 the EU launched the Arctic 
Urban Regional Cooperation (AURC) network, and the Arctic Youth Dialogues, which are partly 
implemented through the EU-funded project Youth Together for Arctic Futures, led by WWF and 
supported by the Norwegian Arctic Council chairship. The Saami Council, a Permanent 
Participant, is part of this project. 
The EU is a major supporter and funder of Arctic research through its Horizon programme (EUR 
115 million for the period 2021-2024) of regional development in the European Arctic through 
Interreg, and supports the education and green economy sectors in Greenland. 
EU ENGAGEMENT IN THE ARCTIC COUNCIL 
During the reporting period, the EU welcomed the transfer of chairship to Norway as well as the 
progressive resumption of work under the Arctic Council and its Working and Expert Groups, and 
Task Forces. The EU, mostly through the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre has 
contributed to their work. The European Commission’s experts provide unique support and bring 
in the vast amount of data and information the EU generates through its own programmes. 
The EU participated in the informal Observers meetings organised in 2023 and 2024 in Warsaw, 
Poland; and the Observers meeting organised in 2024 in Tromsø, Norway. The EU welcomes 
these meetings as very productive. 
PERMANENT PARTICIPANTS 
The Saami Council and the Inuit Circumpolar Council, both Permanent Participants, participate 
in the EU Arctic Forum and Indigenous Peoples’ Dialogue as well as in several Horizon projects. 
The EU also supports the Saami Council, a Permanent Participant, through several grants aimed 
to build capacity and expand knowledge and visibility about Sápmi. 
With the new Commission Office in Greenland, engagement with the ICC is also increasing. 
OTHER WORK 
The EU is engaged in Arctic Council work also through OSPAR (the Convention for the protection 
of the northeast Atlantic marine environment and itself an observer to the Arctic Council) to which 
EU is a Contracting Party. It is expected that in its forthcoming ministerial meeting (June 2025) 
OSPAR will reaffirm its commitment to implement specific actions in the Arctic, including 
identification of priority sites to be considered in developing its network of marine protected areas 
(MPAs) and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs).

The European Commission has been a partner in the Arctic PASSION project supporting 
Sustainable Arctic Observing Networks (SAON) as a work package co-leader, with studies on 
societal benefits of Arctic observing systems and by developing a service on air pollution 
forecasting contributing to the SAON’s initiative to develop the Arctic Global Earth Observation 
System of Systems (GEOSS) representing the regional component. In 2024 the European 
Commission contributed to the implementation of the SAON Roadmap, e.g. through the 
enhancement of existing observations with new data and instrumentation, calibration and 
processing schemes to unify observing protocols, or the establishment of a unified data catalogue 
supporting. 
WORKING GROUPS 
AMAP - Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme: The European Commission represented 
the EU at the AMAP plenary meeting; attended the first meetings of AMAP expert groups on 
mercury and on Persistent Organic Pollutants, and; participated in the EU-funded AMAP working 
group project “Arctic Black Carbon impacting on Climate and Air Pollution (ABC-iCAP)” by taking 
part in the project steering group. The European Commission further collaborated with AMAP 
regarding the JRC activity on Quality Assurance and Quality Control for marine microliter (plastic) 
monitoring, and also participated in Open Ended Science Group (OESG) of Minamata 
Convention on mercury pollution at the global scale including the Arctic and delivered updated 
emission inventories of atmospheric mercury and Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) from the 
Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) contributing to OESG studies 
on mercury. AMAP was also invited to participate in the EU Arctic Forum. 
SDWG - Sustainable Development Working Group: The European Commission represented the 
EU at the SDWG plenary meeting. 
CAFF - Conservation of Arctic Flora and Fauna: The European Commission participated in the 
consultation launched to the experts contributing to the alien species report providing risk 
assessment references. 
PAME - Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment: The European Commission represented 
the EU at the 2024 PAME expert group meeting on marine litter. 
EPPR – Emergency Prevention Preparedness and Response: The European Commission 
represents the EU in the EPPR Working Group, contributed to the WFI, and invited EPPR to 
participate in the EU Arctic Forum. 
EXPERT GROUPS 
EGBCM - Expert Group on Black Carbon and Methane: The European Commission represented 
the EU at the two EGBCM meetings and has contributed to the elaboration of the EGBCM 
Summary report with relevant data on emissions and projections. Work under Arctic PASSION, 
e.g. the ‘Local Atmospheric Pollution Forecast’ service EGBCM (additional information below). 
The European Commission contributes to the work of the Arctic Council through research 
projects funded by the EU. European Commission’s experts provide unique support and bring in 
the vast amount of data and information the EU generates through its own programmes, such as 
Horizon Europe, or through policy-oriented research. It also makes available and free of charge 
the observation data gathered through the Copernicus Programme, which is essential for Arctic 
research, in particular on climate matters. As examples, most recent CORDIS Results Packs 
(2024): 

• Cordis Results Pack : Understanding impacts of climate change on Earth’s vulnerable 
polar regions - European Commission (europa.eu) 

• Diving deeper: Propelling ocean knowledge and its sustainable management (europa.eu) 

• Tackling marine litter from source to sea (europa.eu)

Future plans for contributing to the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task 
Forces, and/or Expert Groups. 
The EU launched a study to identify the indirect impact and contribution its different programmes 
have on the work of the Arctic Council. This study is in its later stages and will help the EU and 
the Arctic Council to further enhance their cooperation.

Other aspects of the Arctic Council and its goals not covered by the previous sections 
The EU's general engagement in Arctic-relevant issues (beyond the Arctic Council) 
The EU engages in many different contexts focusing on Arctic matters or relevant to the Arctic, 
for example the Agreement to prevent unregulated fisheries in the Central Arctic Ocean, or the 
global processes on the Global Biodiversity Framework or the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond 
National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). 
ARCTIC SCIENCE MINISTERIAL 
The EU supports the continuation and the implementation of the Arctic Science Ministerial. 
WILDFIRES 
The EU also support the Chairship’s Wildland Fires Initiative (WFI) through sharing information 
about its own work under the EU’s Civil Protection Mechanism or Copernicus Emergency 
Management Service. The European Commission contributed to the WFI at the wildfire event 
organised by the Norwegian chairship at the Arctic Circle Forum Berlin (May 2024). Through the 
Global Wildfire Information System (GWIS), it provided the elaboration of Daily Maps published 
by DG ECHO. Additionally, the European Commission continuously monitored the AMAP region 
in GWIS, through a specific Arctic-focused analysis. The EU also organised an event on 
Emergency Management in the Arctic at the 2024 EU Arctic Forum, with the participation of the 
Chair of the Arctic Council’s EPPR Working Group as well as the Saami Council. 
BLACK CARBON 
From December 2021 to December 2023, the EU-funded project ‘Arctic Black Carbon impacting 
Climate and Air Pollution (ABC-iCAP)’ contributed to the work of the Arctic Council through 
several activities. The project worked with the Arctic Council's Expert Group on Black Carbon 
and Methane (EGBCM) and the Arctic Council's Working Group on Monitoring and Assessment 
(AMAP). The overall objective was to contribute to global efforts to reduce black carbon and 
methane emissions impacting the Arctic from target countries through awareness raising, 
capacity-building and expert analysis supporting knowledge-sharing and promotion of key 
practices and measures such as monitoring, emission inventories and application of Best 
Available Techniques for key emission sectors. A key strategy was to provide value-added and 
contribution to the work of the UNECE Air Convention and its subsidiary bodies and strengthen 
strategic relations with non-EU Arctic countries – the USA, Canada and Norway. The key 
outcomes of the project include: 

• Five technical reports (Fire in the Arctic: Current Trends and Future Pathways; The Future 
of Arctic Fires: Leveraging Ongoing Activities, New Efforts, and International Cooperation; 
New Products and Data for Better Monitoring of Arctic Black Carbon; Socio-Economic 
Analysis of Air Pollution and Climate Forcer Emission Reductions in the Arctic Council 
Member States with Special Focus on Black Carbon and Methane Emissions; Synthesis 
of Arctic Council Member and Observer Emissions of Black Carbon and Methane) 

• Three training sessions in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan on methane emissions mitigation 
in the oil and gas sector; 

• Three webinars on Arctic wildfires; 

• Facilitation of international cooperation on black carbon and methane emissions 
reduction, including collaboration with IMO on reducing black carbon emissions from 
Arctic shipping and with the UNFCCC on promoting the Global Methane Pledge. 

The project was implemented by the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme (AMAP) 
Secretariat in cooperation with the Finnish Environment Institute (SYKE) and the Swedish 
Environmental Research Institute (IVL).
